findings.where: Phone first screen: the order of photo, heading, yellow address strip and the 'I advise…' paragraph
findings.fault: On a phone the yellow address strip sits right on the fold (about 765–858 px on an 844 px screen), so the first screen cuts the one action in half. The paragraph that says what Mark does and for whom comes after the strip, at the bottom of the frame. A phone visitor's first screen shows a face and an opinion, but not what he offers or a complete way to reach him. The desktop order (line, then what he does, then the address) is lost.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer opening the link from LinkedIn on a phone. They can't tell from the first screen what Mark does for whom, and the contact route is only partly in view.

findings.where: Nav links Profile, Articles and Blog (#profile, #articles, #blog); the article specimen's download link 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' (href #)
findings.fault: The parts map shows these are real links, but none goes anywhere. The page has no Profile, Articles or Blog section to jump to, and the download link points at '#'. A visitor who clicks gets nothing. The download is also labelled as a direct PDF, not as a link to an HTML page that holds the PDF.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who clicks Profile to check Mark's record, or clicks the lecture to read it, and finds the page doesn't move. It reads as broken on a site whose job is to show his work.

findings.where: Navigation in the hero (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The nav has no 'Contact' item. The only route to Mark is the address strip in the hero, so once a visitor scrolls past it or lands on another page, nothing in the standing navigation says how to reach him.
findings.who_objects: A procurement reader who has read further and comes back to get in touch. The nav is where they look first, and it offers no contact.

findings.where: Motion specimen: the 'Replay the entrance' control
findings.fault: It is a button, but it looks like a blue underlined link. It takes the link colour and underline that the rest of the page uses for links that go somewhere.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who expects a blue underline to take them to another page, and finds it plays an animation where they are instead.

findings.where: Article specimen: the title 'The World's Best…' and the body 'world's best PPP law'
findings.fault: The apostrophe in 'World's' is straight, and it shows at display size, while every other quote mark in the article is curly (“ ” ‘ ’).
findings.who_objects: A reader of a page that sells the polish of a legal journal. A straight apostrophe in the headline looks like an unfinished paste.

findings.where: Article specimen: the lectern photograph's grey treatment
findings.fault: The greyscale grade turns the stage backdrop into a large near-black slab. It is the heaviest thing in the article, much heavier than the title and the text, and it breaks up the quiet paper page.
findings.who_objects: A reader of the article. The eye goes to a dark block rather than the argument, against the tile's own 'flat and quiet' paper.

findings.where: Phone hero: the portrait inside the frame
findings.fault: On a phone the portrait floats inside the frame with its own margins, and its left edge doesn't line up with the text column below it. The tile's own concept is a portrait 'set flush against' the document's edge, which the desktop does.
findings.who_objects: The founder judging the direction. The one borrowed detail, the paper's edge with the portrait flush to it, disappears at phone width.

findings.where: Texture specimen: the framed empty box with a part-width yellow bar
findings.fault: The diagram is an empty hairline box with a yellow bar that stops partway across. Without the hero's photo column it reads as a broken or unloaded image, not as a map of the paper and its address strip.
findings.who_objects: The founder reading the tile. The texture section looks unfinished instead of showing the ground's restraint.

findings.where: Hero name 'Mark M. Moseley' against the article byline and tile footer 'Mark Moseley'
findings.fault: His name appears in two forms on one page.
findings.who_objects: Mark, and a reader checking that the author of the article is the advisor in the hero. A personal brand should name the person one way.

findings.where: Article specimen, desktop: the download row's 'Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF'
findings.fault: The date and format are pushed to the far right of the column, apart from the title they describe. On the phone they sit under it. The space between them weakens the pairing.
findings.who_objects: A reader scanning the downloads, who has to look across a gap to see what the file is and when it dates from.
